newsitem.title: USA: Judge opens door to suit on Ill. tollway budget.
newsitem.headline: Judge opens door to suit on Ill. tollway budget.

text.p: A Cook County, Ill., Circuit Court judge has opened the door to a challenge against the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority's ability to spend money independently of legislative approval, according to an attorney representing tollway motorists who filed the lawsuit.

The ruling by Judge Stephen Schiller, released late Friday, rejected a motion by the tollway authority to dismiss the claim brought by a group of tollway motorists in a lawsuit filed last year, said Myron Cherry, their attorney.
Cherry said Monday the judge found the motorists' claim challenging the right of the tollway authority to spend funds without an appropriation by the Illinois General Assembly to be valid.

Cherry said the ruling called into question not only annual spending by the tollway authority, but also the legality of its bonding practices. In a news release, he pointed out that the authority has issued hundreds of millions of debt for projects "that have not initially been sanctioned or approved by the required constitutional General Assembly process."
Julian D'Esposito, the tollway authority's chairman, said Monday that the case lacks merit and that a motion would be filed for reconsideration of Schiller's ruling.

He said the tollway authority has "plenty of legislative oversight," but does not derive its revenues from state general funds that need to be appropriated by the legislature. Instead, the authority is solely funded through toll revenues it collects.
In his news release, Cherry said that the ruling also calls into question the authority's planned multi-billion-dollar bond-financed expansion program.
But, D'Esposito said it was unclear what Schiller's ruling would mean for future bond sales.

The motorists' lawsuit had claimed the authority was collecting millions of dollars in toll revenues each year and spending the money without oversight from the General Assembly in violation of the Illinois Constitution.

Another count in the lawsuit, which claimed the authority lacked proper legislative authority to build and finance new toll roads, was dismissed with prejudice by Schiller. The lawsuit had asked the court to order the authority to develop and implement a plan for merging existing toll roads into the state's freeway system.

Meanwhile another lawsuit, challenging the validity of an environmental impact statement for a 12.5-mile extension of the tollway system in northeastern Illinois, is still pending in U.S. District Court in Chicago.

Robert Michaels, staff attorney for the Chicago-based Environmental Law & Policy Center, which filed the lawsuit along with other groups, said Monday that Judge Suzanne Conlon has set a briefing schedule on a motion for summary judgement in the case. That schedule calls for the case to be fully briefed by Dec. 12, Michaels said.

Just days after the group filed the lawsuit, Gov. Jim Edgar approved the south extension of I-355 from DuPage County into Will County. An approximately $600 million revenue bond issue has been planned by the authority to finance the project.

D'Esposito said the tollway authority has told the court it does not plan to award any contracts for the expansion or issue any bonds until after Jan. 30. He declined to speculate what the authority would do if Conlon has not decided the case by then.
